justification_text:
My point estimates reflected a modest upward drift from what I understood to be the prevailing S&P 500 level near 3,000–3,030 at the time of the forecast. For the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the last known price and applied only a small positive drift, consistent with the historical daily average return of roughly 0.03–0.05%. The one-week and one-month estimates incorporated slightly more cumulative drift while also acknowledging mean-reversion tendencies and the fact that markets don't trend strongly in any single direction over short periods without a clear catalyst. The gentle upward slope across horizons reflects the long-run equity risk premium rather than any specific bullish signal.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to historical volatility. The S&P 500 has an annualized volatility of roughly 15–20%, which translates to daily moves of about 1% and weekly moves of roughly 2–3%. My one-day interval of roughly ±68 points represents about ±2.2% at a 90% confidence level, which is somewhat tighter than pure historical vol would suggest, reflecting that very large single-day moves are relatively rare in calm regimes. The one-month interval of ±325 points around 3,075 reflects the wider cone of uncertainty that accumulates over four weeks, where macro data, earnings reports, and sentiment shifts can compound meaningfully.

The most significant tail risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include an unexpected Federal Reserve policy surprise, a geopolitical shock such as an escalation in a major conflict, or a sudden deterioration in credit markets signaling systemic stress. On the upside, a major positive catalyst like a breakthrough trade deal, stronger-than-expected employment or GDP data, or a dovish pivot from central banks could push the index well above my upper bounds. These are low-probability but high-impact events that fat-tailed distributions would capture better than a simple normal approximation.

It's also worth noting that my forecast was generated without real-time data, so if the market had already moved significantly by the time this forecast was consumed, the stated intervals could be miscalibrated. Regime changes — such as a transition from low-volatility to high-volatility environments — are particularly hard to anticipate and represent a structural risk to the reliability of any short-horizon confidence interval built on historical patterns.
